name: Violet ray hair-growth comb electrode

card.summary: A comb-shaped glass attachment for a violet-ray (high-frequency) device, drawn across the scalp in the hope of stimulating hair growth.
card.aka: Violet ray comb; high-frequency comb electrode; Tesla comb
card.note: Violet-ray devices were the subject of US seizures and lawsuits in the 1940s and 1950s; modern users report ozone odour and recommend caution with implants.

quick.overview:
The comb electrode is a glass attachment for a violet-ray device, a handheld high-voltage, high-frequency, low-current unit from the early twentieth century. The comb is passed over the scalp, producing a faint glow and tingling, and users hope it stimulates the follicles to thicken or regrow hair.

Original violet-ray makers marketed the devices for many complaints, and modern high-frequency comb attachments are sold online for scalp care. Forum users describe regrowth anecdotes; no controlled trials of the comb attachment were identified.
quick.how: Users move the glass comb or other tube over the scalp for a few minutes at a time, usually repeated over weeks, and combine it with other hair treatments. Modern electrodes are sold as replacement attachments for high-frequency facial devices.
quick.risks: Forum posts mention an ozone smell and respiratory irritation in some users, and consumer guides list pacemakers, pregnancy and autoimmune disease as reasons to avoid it. Historically, US authorities took action against violet-ray manufacturers in the 1940s and 1950s.

lead: A violet-ray comb electrode is a glass, comb-shaped applicator that fits the handle of a violet-ray device. Violet rays were electrotherapy units that used a coil to deliver high-voltage, high-frequency, low-current electricity through evacuated glass tubes of different shapes, including surface and nasal electrodes.[1]

As a hair treatment, practitioners and users move the comb over the scalp in the belief that it stimulates circulation and the follicles. Modern sellers describe the attachments as 'high-frequency' combs, some using neon gas, for scalp care and hair growth.[2]

Most American antique units were made before the Depression by firms such as Renulife, Fitzgerald and Fisher, and in the 1940s and 1950s manufacturers faced lawsuits, recalls and seizures; Master Electric, described as the last US maker, was sued in 1951.[1]

chain: Glass electrode delivers a high-frequency current to the scalp
Users believe follicles and scalp circulation are stimulated
Possible thicker or regrown hair, as claimed by users
angle.text: Users run the comb over thinning areas in the hope of improving density. Reports come from users and sellers rather than trials.

paras: The violet-ray set consists of a control box with an interrupter and a handle holding a high-voltage coil; interchangeable evacuated glass tubes are inserted into the handle.[1] Comb-shaped electrodes pass through hair and contact the scalp, while other tubes are used on the face or body.[1]

Violet-ray devices were widely sold in the early twentieth century, with a prototype often attributed to Nikola Tesla's 1893 demonstration, a claim that encyclopedic sources mark as needing citation.[1] After the Depression, many makers moved to radio coils and other electrical components during the Second World War.[1]
In the 1940s and 1950s, violet-ray makers faced lawsuits and government actions including recalls, seizures and destruction orders.[1]
No studies found. Online hair-loss forum threads discuss historical and modern electrical-stimulation studies and users' personal results, which are anecdotal rather than controlled.[3]

Modern retailers sell replacement comb electrodes for high-frequency devices, and consumer articles describe the devices for scalp health while noting that more research and human trials are needed.[2][3] Forum users describe regrowth on treated areas and also mention ozone produced by the device.[3]

timeline.event: Tesla's high-frequency apparatus is often cited as the origin of the violet ray (claim noted as unsourced).[1]
Master Electric is sued; the FDA seizes devices.[1]
